Press Release:


Jayde’s Family Speaks
Christopher Panayiotou, the Port Elizabeth businessman accused of masterminding his wife Jayde’s murder in April, has applied for bail for a second time. He now waits for the Grahamstown High Court’s decision next Tuesday. But so too does Jayde’s family. Carte Blanche sits down with Jayde’s mother Michelle and sister Toni to hear of their anguish over losing Jayde.


Script:


Jayde’s family speaks


VO: 28”
This photo shoot was a gift from Jayde Panayoitou to her parents Derick and Michelle and her sister Toni Inggs for Christmas last year – they were taken on the family farm and speak volumes about the deep connection this family had. It was their first and last family photo shoot.

John:
At six thirty in the morning on the 21st of April, Jayde was standing outside her complex in Port Elizabeth waiting for a colleague to give her a lift to school. When her colleague arrived she wasn’t here and fears began to grow that she had been abducted. Shortly afterwards she was reported missing.

VO:
It’s a day her mother will never forget.

Michelle:
As the hours were going by and there was no news or no sign of her, I kept hoping obviously that it would just be a robbery, kidnap and and we’d find her.

VO: 8”
It was equally surreal to her sister Toni who took to facebook and posted this message to raise awareness.

Toni:
I can’t even explain the feeling, my heart just dropped to my toes. I was busy raising a little baboon, because I was doing animal rehabilitation at the time. So I had this little baboon with me and I wrapped her in my jacket, told my mom to put on something and we raced through to PE. We all met at the house and it was like okay... now what do we do, where do we start?

VO: 8”
That first night Toni and her mother sat worrying while her father and her husband Christopher joined the police and the search parties.

Michelle:
It was very cold that night, I remember it and me and Toni and my niece we were sitting in the lounge, we got the blankets out, watching TV. We didn’t know what else to do with ourselves and every time I put the blanket over myself I threw it off because I thought, well Jayde could be lying somewhere freezing cold, alive and I’m all cuddled with a blanket in my home.

VO: 5
Toni remembers comforting Jayde’s husband, Chris throughout that night.

Toni:
I was up all night chatting to Chris. 'Cos, like I said, he did mean a lot to me. He was my brother-in-law, and I was on the phone with him all night, I was really worried about him. I was more concerned about him than I was about my own family because I’ve got my Mom and Dad and although he’s got his family, he’s going home alone. That broke my heart... my heart was really broken for him.

VO: 4”
During this time they clung to the hope that Jayde would be found.

Toni:
I remember thinking it’s fine, she can be raped, she can be hurt, they could have really badly hurt her, they must just dump her somewhere now and she’ll find her way to a light or something. I had so much hope in that, that I convinced myself that that was the case, and that someone would be driving along the road and that they would see her.

John:
Because you could have rebuilt from there, I guess?

Could lose Toni:
Yes because anything that is broken can be fixed.

VO: 7”
But the following day she was found murdered, her body abandoned on a farm outside her home town of Uitenhage.

Michelle.
I’ve been told that I fainted in the kitchen and I don’t remember anything after that. Of that. I do recall the doctor coming to give me an injection to calm me down, but these are all things that I have been told because I don’t remember anything and then when I did wake up it was just surreal. It’s just not right, this is not happening.

VO: 3”
Then came the news of an arrest.

Michelle:
My husband got the phone call that an arrest had been made, but they didn’t tell us who it was.

Toni:
I was so overjoyed. I was so happy. The first thing I did was pick up my phone and send Chris a message - Chris have you spoken to the cops tonight?, to tell him someone’s been arrested. And the message didn’t deliver and something just sparked in me; something is going on here and I didn’t know what. And the whole night I was sending him messages and nothing was going through and by the next morning I just knew it was him that had been arrested.

VO: 10”
Initially her friends battled with the notion that Chris could be behind the alleged crime. Especially her lifelong friend who she had started school with, Kerry Lee Connarchan.

Kerry Lee:
If someone asks me now about Christopher I say he was a cuddly teddy bear. You wouldn’t think that he’d do something like this. I still, when it actually happened, I said to my mom... the whole time I said 'Mom it can’t be Chris'.

VO 3”:
The family felt betrayed by Chris’s silence.

Toni:
An innocent person does not act that way. He would have turned around and contacted us somehow or said to his family, like phone my other mom and dad, tell Toni, tell them I am innocent, I didn’t do this. He hasn’t once tried to do that.

VO: 12”
Then reports started surfacing in the media suggesting that the motive might have been an affair with his co-worker Chanelle Coutts, and rumours surfaced that Chris may have paid a hit man to kill Jayde.

Toni:
And then it was just disgust, more than anything else. We were just disgusted.

Michelle:
Who does that? Which normal person does things like that? I’m not used to things like that; it doesn’t happen in my family.

Toni:
My sister would be so embarrassed, I say this to everybody, she would be so embarrassed. More than anything else and that is heartbreaking for me. She was such a good wife.

VO: 18:
Christopher was arrested along with a bouncer from his nightclub Luthando Siyole and the alleged hit man, Sizwe Vumazonke.


Nothing could prepare the family for the massive outpouring of support from around the globe that followed.

Michelle:
I have so many thank you’s for so many people now where at first it was we’re not those type of people, we’re very private people. But I’ve had to come to terms with that; it's not private anymore, this is a case that is all over the newspapers. I appreciate every single hug, every single comment from the total strangers that I have never even met or seen.

John link:
The town of Uitenhage is still reeling from the murder of Jayde, but now a small group of her friends are trying to honour her memory by completing her bucket list.

VO: 9”
On the Facebook page created in support of Jayde dozens of people, some friends, some complete strangers, have helped fulfill the young teacher’s simple list.

Kerry Lee:
I want to try to do all of them. Being a close friend of Jayde, there’s many that I want to do. We’re actually going now - in the first weekend of August - we, my boyfriend and I, we’re climbing the Cockscomb Mountain and I want to do that hike for Jayde, and I want to carry something with me for her.

VO: 5”
While Jayde’s death has drawn many people together, it’s also torn the two families apart.

John:
His guilt or innocence is yet to be proven in a court, but has it been difficult for you seeing Chris in court?

Toni:
The first time it was very difficult, it was literally like an out of body experience, because the last time I saw him I was giving him a hug and kiss goodbye. He was off to his parents' house; that was the night he was arrested. He’d just had supper with my family. He slept in my sister’s bed for the week after everything had happened. Going from that - from me still loving this guy as my brother-in-law - to seeing him in court... I can’t explain in words the feeling.


Michelle:
When I saw them the first time I looked at all three of them as they came into the dock, and I did turn away because I got very emotional. But afterwards I did turn around and I watched. It was upsetting, but I have to see him, and I have to just give my anger to him, even if it's just the way I look at him.

VO:
It’s a mother’s cry for remorse.

Michelle:
We were part of their lives for 11 years, part of their family, they were part of our family for 11 years. It still comes down to the point that my daughter has been murdered - who they loved, apparently, but have shown no mercy towards us.

John:
Is there something they could have done differently? What would have changed that relationship?

Could shorten Michelle:
Just a whatsapp message. How are you doing? How are you coping and they haven’t. But I’ve written them off. They mustn’t come to me now. They’ve had three months, three months to send me a word and they haven’t.



VO:
The Panayoitou family this week declined to comment.

VO: 10 ”
In June Christopher was denied bail in the PE courts. This week he made a renewed bid for bail in the Grahamstown High Court, appealing the earlier decision. His defence team argued that he was not a flight risk and also cited heinous jail conditions at St Albans prison. In his affidavit Chris has maintained his innocence and says he has nothing to gain from Jayde’s murder.

John:
What would you like to see happen with the bail appeal when court convenes on Tuesday? How would you like that process to end?

Michelle:
No bail

John:
No bail?

Michelle:
Simple as that. No bail. And if he gets no bail he’ll go to Bloemfontein to the Supreme Courts. He’s welcome…I’ll be there too in Bloemfontein.

VO: 6:
For Toni the greatest betrayal remains that Jayde’s murder was the fulfillment of her worst fear.

Toni:
My sister's biggest fear was either to be alone at home and someone breaking in and hurting her or being taken and getting hurt. And that’s what makes this whole thing even worse.

VO: 6”
Toni’s started a campaign and says she won’t rest until she sees justice for Jayde.

Toni:
I’ve always been one of those who complain about South Africa and how things go here and how badly I want to get out of South Africa, but after this the whole perspective has changed. Rather than complaining, get up and do something about it – that’s exactly what I am doing now.

VO: 4
And only then will her mother be able to find closure.

Michelle:
I need to get on with mourning my daughter and that’s what I am finding really difficult right now, because all the focus is on Christopher.


10 sec Promo 1:

VO:
In a heartfelt interview three months after the senseless murder of her daughter Jayde, Michelle Inggs speaks exclusively to Carte Blanche about her pain and anger.



15 sec Promo 2:

VO:
This week Christopher Panyoitou who stands accused of murdering his wife Jayde launched a renewed bid for bail. We speak exclusively to Jayde’s mother, her sister and her best friend. The tragedy has galvanized them to seek justice for Jayde.


Promo 3:

VO:
In an exclusive interview Michelle Inggs, the mother of murdered Eastern Cape school teacher Jayde Panayoitou, shares the pain and the anger that has engulfed her over the past three months. She’s determined to see justice for her beloved daughter.

He’s welcome…I’ll be there too in Bloemfontein. VO: 6: For Toni the greatest betrayal remains that Jayde’s murder was the fulfillment of her worst fear. Toni: My sister's biggest fear was either to be alone at home and someone breaking in and hurting her or being taken and getting hurt. And that’s what makes this whole thing even worse. VO: 6” Toni’s started a campaign and says she won’t rest until she sees justice for Jayde. Toni: I’ve always been one of those who complain about South Africa and how things go here and how badly I want to get out of South Africa, but after this the whole perspective has changed. Rather than complaining, get up and do something about it – that’s exactly what I am doing now. VO: 4 And only then will her mother be able to find closure. Michelle: I need to get on with mourning my daughter and that’s what I am finding really difficult right now, because all the focus is on Christopher. 10 sec Promo 1: VO: In a heartfelt interview three months after the senseless murder of her daughter Jayde, Michelle Inggs speaks exclusively to Carte Blanche about her pain and anger. 15 sec Promo 2: VO: This week Christopher Panyoitou who stands accused of murdering his wife Jayde launched a renewed bid for bail. We speak exclusively to Jayde’s mother, her sister and her best friend. The tragedy has galvanized them to seek justice for Jayde. Promo 3: VO: In an exclusive interview Michelle Inggs, the mother of murdered Eastern Cape school teacher Jayde Panayoitou, shares the pain and the anger that has engulfed her over the past three months. She’s determined to see justice for her beloved daughter.
